Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow. Certain words have been printed in bold to help you locate them.
In 2024, a young Indian venture called The Bio Company (TBC) walked away with the Best Innovation in Textile prize at the PETA Vegan Fashion Awards. What earned it the award was an unlikely claim: shoes and bags made out of tomatoes. Its founder, Pritesh Mistry, was twenty-six at the time, and the brand he had built, Bioleather, uses tomatoes as its primary raw material through a process that avoids polyurethane (PU) and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) altogether.
But why tomatoes? The answer lies in arithmetic rather than sentiment. India is the second-largest producer of tomatoes in the world, growing roughly 44 million tonnes a year, and somewhere between 30 and 35 per cent of that produce never gets eaten. Mistry has said plainly that this enormous quantity of waste was among the chief reasons the crop was chosen. Skins and seeds, the bulk of what is thrown away, turn out to be a dependable and readily available input. Tomatoes also happen to be rich in pectin, a natural polymer that lends the finished sheet both flexibility and strength, while their fibrous structure and natural oils give it a leather-like feel without costing it its biodegradability. One intervention therefore takes on two separate problems: food that rots uneaten, and the pollution long associated with conventional leather.
The idea took shape while Mistry was studying biotechnology in Mumbai. Trips to farms during those years showed him how much food was being lost; visits linked to the leather trade showed him the pollution that ordinary processing leaves behind. Between the two, he began looking for a material that could put agricultural waste to productive use. Turning that thought into Bioleather demanded considerable experimentation — months spent on tomato by-products, one formulation after another, adjusting texture and durability until the sheet resembled leather while staying sustainable and biodegradable.
Since 2018 the company has pushed towards an affordable Bioleather that is vegan, carbon-neutral and biodegradable, coloured with natural dyes; both the technology and the process behind it have been patented. Raw material is sourced from food-processing units and farms in tomato-growing belts such as Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh, where produce that would otherwise be discarded is instead gathered and repurposed for Bioleather. At the firm's Surat facility the by-products are mixed with biopolymers, plant-based binders and natural fibres, then put through a non-toxic curing process that builds strength, durability and a leather-like texture. A plant-based coating applied at the end improves water resistance, and the sheet that emerges carries no PU or PVC and remains biodegradable.
Interest has come from fashion, accessories and, more recently, the automobile sector. Sustainable labels have turned the material into jackets, bags and footwear, while carmakers are examining it for interiors and upholstery. Asked the question buyers ask most often — whether it smells like leather — Mistry describes the scent as pleasant and neutral, free of the plastic or chemical odour that synthetic leather tends to carry. The Surat unit currently turns out about 5,000 metres of Bioleather a month, a capacity Mistry calls scalable; as demand grows the company means to raise output without letting quality or sustainability slip.

What can be inferred about Mistry's approach from the passage?
options: It prioritises profit over environmental concerns.
It depends entirely on government subsidies to survive.
It attempts to combine waste reduction with sustainable material innovation.
It seeks to replace the entire leather industry within a few years.
It has abandoned commercial production in favour of research.
